children: Oil prices rose and U.S. stock futures

declined Sunday evening after President Donald Trump rejected Iran’s latest proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, putting renewed pressure on markets already contending with high interest rates and inflation concerns.

) and Nasdaq 100 futures each fell about 0.3% in early Asian trading.

The renewed rise in oil threatens to keep inflation elevated just as investors are bracing for another Federal Reserve rate increase. Higher energy prices can raise costs across the economy, squeeze corporate profit margins and make it harder for the Fed to bring inflation under control. That combination could keep bond yields elevated and put additional pressure on stock valuations.

Global borrowing costs are already climbing. The average yield on a broad measure of global bonds moved above 4% last week for the first time since 2007, increasing concerns that expensive credit could eventually slow economic growth and hurt corporate earnings.
Hormuz remains the market’s pressure point

The Strait of Hormuz remains central to the market outlook because of its importance to global energy shipments. Iran has proposed reopening the waterway within seven days, but Washington rejected Tehran’s latest terms.

Trump nevertheless said he expects negotiations with Iran to resume this week, according to Axios. He also said he is seriously considering restrictions on U.S. diesel exports, another potential source of uncertainty for energy markets.
Fed policy adds another layer of risk
Several Federal Reserve officials have cited solid economic growth and a resilient labor market as reasons interest rates may need to rise further. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack
to fiscal concerns as one factor pushing longer-term Treasury yields higher.
Traders are pricing in at least one additional quarter-point Fed increase before the end of the year.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent offered a less hawkish view, arguing that policymakers should remain flexible because productivity improvements from artificial intelligence and deregulation could help restrain inflation.

Investors will get fresh evidence this week from the Fed’s preferred inflation measure and U.S. employment reports. Those releases could determine whether expectations for another rate increase strengthen or ease.

For now, oil remains the crucial variable. A sustained increase in crude prices could reinforce inflation fears, push bond yields higher and complicate the outlook for stocks. Progress toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz could ease some of those pressures.
